questions: Why do we divide the total by 9 and not by 20, the top mark?
Where will the mean marker stop, and how do you know?
segments.say: Nine scores, one dot each. Count the dots as they land and add the scores with me: the total is 90 over nine students. Keep your student notes open at the mean definition for this scene.

questions: Which marker found the middle dot, and which dot was it?
Why is the mode 8 and not 10?
segments.say: Three centres: mean 10, median 9, mode 8. Three markers, three different centres, one data set. Check the median and mode definitions in your student notes and say them back to your partner.

questions: What changed in the data, and what changed in the total?
Why did the median stay at 9 when the biggest score moved?
segments.say: The mean follows the outlier; the median resists. I drag the top score from 18 to 27 and the mean chases it to 11, but the median ring never moves. Now try the outlier question on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: Why does the class 20-30 use 25 in the f x column?
What does the cumulative entry 16 actually count?
segments.say: Grouped data: the cumulative frequency table. Each class is represented by its midpoint, the f x column builds to 600, and the cumulative column climbs 2, 8, 16, 22, 24.

questions: Why do we plot at the upper class boundary and not the midpoint here?
Why does the curve climb steeply in the middle classes?
segments.say: The ogive: cumulative frequency curve. The table becomes a curve: upper class boundaries across, cumulative frequencies up, and the probe joins the points into the ogive.

questions: Why do we read the median at cumulative frequency 12 and not at 24?
What does the interquartile range tell us that the range does not?
segments.say: Read-off: median about 25, IQR about 16.7. Half of 24 is 12 - across to the curve, down to the axis. The same move from 6 and 18 gives the two quartiles.

questions: Where does the beam balance, and which centre is that?
When an outlier is present, which two centres will you report together?
segments.say: The mean is the balance point, not the tallest bar. Slide the fulcrum until the beam balances: it settles under 10, the mean, nowhere near the tallest bar. Then take the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits exactly this claim.
segments.watchFor: The mean always describes the typical score. Listen for it in pair talk and watch for it on the exit ticket: One extreme score drags the mean away from the bulk of the data. Send them back to the dragged dot and the balance beam and the correct turn: The mean follows the outlier, the median resists it: report both when an outlier is present.
